header:
Date: 2026-07-24
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jonah Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (CTO, Starlake), Alex Gomez (Infra Lead), Liam O'Connor (PM)
summary: High-level discovery focused on per-token economics, batching/caching levers, and choosing between hosted, dedicated, and private deployment given Starlake's strict residency and latency constraints. Starlake is evaluating a pilot; main constraints are 95th percentile latency < 220ms for 512-token responses, strict EU data residency, and a fixed Q3 pilot budget ~ $35k. Discussion covered expected unit costs with/without KV caching, potential dedicated pool sizing, and what Redwood needs to run an initial benchmark using Starlake's prompt corpus.
topics: Intro/qual - stack & constraints; Pricing buckets (hosted/dedicated/private); Batching & KV cache impact; Quantization and model choices; Security/compliance questions; Pilot scope and next steps
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're gonna run through econ and hosting options, i'll hand off to jonah for the perf bits.
[00:12] Priya (Starlake): thanks maya, quick context, we're replatforming our conversational ops and have a hard budget for q3, want to understand cost per call and whether we can do private due to eu residency.
[00:25] Jonah (Redwood SE): cool, can you describe target latency and typical response length?
[00:30] Priya: mostly 300-700 token responses, but the critical flows are 350 to 512 tokens. target 95th < 220ms end-to-end, that's strict.
[00:42] Alex: and we have about 600 concurrent users at peak hitting inference APIs, roughly 4 reqs/sec sustained across the fleet.
[00:50] Maya: ok, so budget wise what's the q3 envelope?
[00:54] Liam: we carved out around 35k USD for the pilot phase, might stretch to 45k if the numbers make sense.
[00:59] Jonah: quick primer — per-token pricing depends on model + runtime. hosted is simplest, lower friction, dedicated gives predictable throughput and lower per-token if you commit, private adds infra/ops cost but meets residency. batching and KV prefix caching dramatically cut per-token cost for repeat or multi-turn workflows.
[01:18] Priya: when you say dramatically — can you give a percent? ballpark?
[01:22] Jonah: ballpark, with modest batching and a working kv cache we often see 30-60% token-cost reduction for our customer corpora; numbers vary. for 512-token averages you'll see the benefit mostly on long multi-turns where kv cache avoids recomputing prefixes.
[01:38] Maya: also quantization — using an int8 or int4 path for compatible models can reduce GPU consumption, which translates to lower per-token unit pricing on Dedicated or Private. Hosted model catalog includes quantized variants we test, but some enterprise customers want private to pin a specific quantized build.
[01:56] Alex: a concern — quantization often degrades quality, do you have evals?
[02:01] Jonah: yes, we run evals and can attach delta quality metrics to the pilot. we'll run their prompts through 1) float16 baseline, 2) int8, 3) int4 when available — show perplexity, rouge, and a small human spot check.
[02:20] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[02:28] Priya: can you explain dedicated sizing? if we need 600 concurrent users and 4 reqs/sec, what does that map to?
[02:36] Jonah: rough calc — depends on model and sequence length. as an example, if we use a 8k-parameter-ish open model equivalent and modest caching, you might need a small pool— say 2-3 high-memory GPUs for baseline throughput, or larger if no caching. dedicated reservations give you predictable throughput and lower per-token rates once committed.
[02:55] Priya: are there cost cliffs between hosted and dedicated?
[02:59] Maya: hosted is pay-as-you-go per-token; dedicated is a monthly committed pool so unit price goes down as volume increases. the cliff is primarily if you can commit to heavy sustained volume — then dedicated wins. for pilots we're flexible — we can simulate dedicated pricing for the pilot to compare.
[03:14] Liam: residency — private deploy is the only real option for us, or a hosted EU-only with strict contracts. is Redwood private fully air-gapped?
[03:23] Jonah: our private mode can be deployed into a customer VPC or on-prem — not necessarily air-gapped by default, but it's designed to integrate with customer KMS/HSM and meet residency. we can provide an on-prem bundle if you need full isolation.
[03:36] Alex: audit logs — do you capture token-level audit logs? we need traceability for compliance.
[03:41] Maya: yes, we provide audit logs, RBAC, SSO/SAML; for Private deployments logs can be routed to your ELK or SIEM; we also have long-term retention addons.
[03:51] Priya: ok great. can we talk numbers — what's a hosted per-token baseline for a generation of 512 tokens?
[03:57] Jonah: i'll give a back-of-envelope: hosted for a medium-sized open model ranges from $0.0006 to $0.002 per token depending on model + streaming vs non-streaming; that would put a 512-token response in the $0.31 - $1.02 range. with batching and caching you can reduce effective spend — e.g., a 40% reduction would bring that $0.60 midpoint to about $0.36.
[04:20] Priya: that feels high for our budget, how do customers scale down cost?
[04:24] Jonah: levers — prefix/KV caching (avoids re-generation for repeated context), batching (amortizes fixed kernel costs across tokens), quantized model variants, routing cheaper model variants for lower criticality flows, and token budgeting (truncate output or parameterize length).
[04:39] Alex: does Redwood offer smart routing so we can mix hosted and private? like keep PII flows in private and route low-risk traffic to hosted?
[04:46] Maya: yes, smart routing by policy is supported — you can define flows by route/metadata and route to hosted/dedicated/private or fallback variants. that's one of the platform differentiators.
[04:56] Liam: about batching — does batching increase tail latency? we need tight 95th percentiles.
[05:02] Jonah: continuous batching is workload-aware; it's tuned to keep tail latency within SLOs. there is a tradeoff: aggressive batch windows lower per-token cost but can add ms of latency. we can tune target batch latency and the runtime will adapt. for your 220ms SLO we would probably use modest batching and aggressive KV hit rates.
[05:20] Alex: sample prompt set — what do you need from us to run a realistic sim?
[05:24] Jonah: ideally 1k prompts representative of your top flows, annotated with expected context sizes and whether user info is PII. we need a small label indicating which flows are latency-critical.
[05:34] Priya: can you also show a model fallback plan if our primary region is constrained?
[05:38] Maya: yes we support fallback policies; you can fallback to a compatible model variant in another region or to a cheaper variant in same region with automatic routing and metrics to track regressions.
[05:49] Speaker 2 (background): um-huh
[05:51] Priya: one of our concerns is quality regression when using quantized or cheaper models — is there a way to automate regression alerts?
[05:57] Jonah: Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring tied to prompt sets; we can set up regression alerts for prompt buckets and roll back rollouts automatically if quality drops beyond threshold.
[06:08] Liam: procurement question — what's the cadence for a pilot invoice? monthly or up front?
[06:12] Maya: pilots are flexible — we do monthly billing for hosted usage, and for dedicated/private pilots we typically agree a short-term commitment with monthly invoicing. details in the pilot contract.
[06:20] Alex: curious — competitor question, we looked at OtherCloudAI, they said their dedicated pools require a six-month commit. what's Redwood's minimum?
[06:27] Maya: no fixed industry-standard here — for Dedicated we often do three-month minimums for pilots but can flex down to one month for smaller pilots. Open to negotiating for pilots.
[06:37] Priya: timeline — if we greenlight this, how quickly can we get a private pilot up?
[06:42] Jonah: with VPC-based private, typically 2-4 weeks for initial deployment and integration depending on access and KMS onboarding; on-prem takes longer. for a hosted pilot it's immediate.
[06:52] Liam: can you quantify expected per-token with private compared to hosted?
[06:56] Jonah: private adds infra ops and infra costs; but if you run your own pooled GPU and we deploy runtime there, per-token can be lower at scale. example: hosted $0.0012/token for a given model, private with your committed pool may yield ~$0.0005-0.0008/token depending on utilization. again, heavy caveats on model and quantization.
[07:18] Priya: ok those example ranges help. can we run two quick scenarios in the pilot: 1) hosted EU-only with strict contract and 2) private VPC. we want cost comparison and a small perf bench.
[07:29] Maya: yes we can. jonah will run bench and i'll package pricing.
[07:33] Jonah: when i run the bench i'll include: a) baseline float16 throughput and latency, b) int8 int4 variants if available, c) batching knob sweep, d) kv-cache hit-rate sensitivity (0%, 30%, 60%).
[07:46] Alex: what KV cache implementation? is it local to runtime or external redis?
[07:50] Jonah: our runtime supports in-memory prefix caching and optional external KV store (redis/managed). MVN — sorry, my bad — memcached/redis are common. for persistence across pods we recommend managed redis.
[07:59] Priya: any gotchas for multi-tenant hosted with EU residency? like data replication?
[08:04] Maya: we can guarantee region-local processing and specific contract terms; data handling depends on plan — private gives you most control. hosted EU-only is possible but some customers prefer private for total control.
[08:14] Liam: ok final recap?
[08:17] Maya: recap — starlake will share 1k sample prompts and latency SLO, redwood to run bench matrix and send hosted/dedicated/private pilot pricing. timeline: pricing by 7/29, bench by 7/30, starlake to decide pilot by end of week of 8/2.
[08:30] Priya: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[08:33] Jonah: thanks all, i'll follow up with a short tech appendix.
[08:36] Meeting ends
